title: On‑Prem VPC Networking Terraform runbook (draft)
content:
Draft notes and runnable guidance for on-prem/VPC networking Terraform modules focused on private DNS, ingress/egress, NAT, firewall rules and K8s network policies.

Purpose:
- Create a single Terraform-first runbook that teams can use to provision and upgrade customer private deployments (VPC or on-prem equivalents) without ad-hoc network edits.
- Capture safe upgrade steps, testing, and rollback for changes that affect egress, DNS resolution, and firewall rules.

Scope (what this doc covers):
- Terraform module layout and naming conventions for VPC, private DNS zones, NAT/egress, firewall appliances/security groups, and K8s network policy bootstrap.
- Upgrade and rollout plan for module releases that touch routing, NAT, and DNS.
- Test plan (terratest/integ/smoke) and rollback actions.

Assumptions / constraints:
- Customers run on one of: AWS (VPC + Route53 private zones), GCP (VPC + CloudDNS private zones), Azure (VNet + Private DNS), or an on-prem network with BIND/CoreDNS managed by ops.
- We will support a provider-aliased multi-target approach in modules (aws, google, azurerm).
- State is stored centrally per-customer in S3/remote backend or on-prem equivalent; state locking must be enabled (DynamoDB/Consul).

High-level proposed modules (TF module names):
- redwood/vpc (inputs: name, cidr_block, azs, public_subnets, private_subnets, nat_gateway_policy)
- redwood/private-dns (inputs: domain, vpc_ids, forwarders (optional), dns_provider)
- redwood/egress-nat (inputs: egress_mode: [centralized, per-subnet], nat_count, nat_type: [managed, instance])
- redwood/firewall (inputs: allowed_ingress, allowed_egress, logging_bucket, appliance_integration)
- redwood/k8s-networkpolicies (bootstrap: default-deny, app-labels, egress-exceptions)
- redwood/peering-transit (optional transit/peering configs)

Module design notes and conventions:
- Variables: use snake_case, prefix module-level variables with module_ when ambiguous. Example: module.vpc.name -> var.name. Keep var names short but explicit.
- Outputs: expose ids and ARNs/URNs: vpc_id, public_subnet_ids, private_subnet_ids, nat_gateway_ids, route_table_ids, private_dns_zone_id.
- Versioning: semantic versioning per module; breaking changes should increment major and require opt-in via module pinning.
- Provider aliasing: modules must accept providers map and documented provider alias usage for multi-region/account.
- IAM & least privilege: modules should produce policy templates but not attach to customer-managed roles unless explicitly opted in.

Example module usage (AWS private DNS association):
```
module "private_dns" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-infra/tf-modules.git//private-dns?ref=v0.3.0"
  providers = { aws = aws.customer }
  domain = "svc.internal.redwood.example"
  vpc_ids = module.vpc.vpc_id
  forwarders = ["10.10.1.2"] # for on-prem forwarding
}
```

Private DNS specifics (patterns we need to cover):
- AWS: create aws_route53_zone (private), aws_route53_zone_association for each VPC. Use cross-account delegations when necessary.
- GCP: private managed zone + dns peering to VPC.
- Azure: private DNS zones and virtual network links.
- On-prem (customer-managed): install CoreDNS instances (daemonset), use stub domains to forward r53/private-zone names to cloud resolver IPs or a shared forwarding appliance.
- Key ops note: never overwrite an existing zone without explicit confirm step in the runbook; prefer to create subdomain for redwood-managed hostnames.

NAT / egress patterns and trade-offs:
- Centralized NAT gateway (per-AZ HA pair) vs per-subnet NAT: centralized is cheaper for many small subnets; per-subnet gives predictable SNAT mapping for auditing.
- AWS managed NAT GW vs NAT instances: prefer managed for production; use instances only in constrained on-prem cases.
- For on-prem we document two patterns: egress via appliance (F5/Checkpoint) with static SNAT ranges, or egress through a cloud-managed VPN + NAT in cloud.
- Egress policy: prefer HTTPS proxy (squid/forward proxy) for allowlists and TLS inspection, fall back to NAT-only where customer prohibits proxy.

Firewall and route rules (templates):
- Perimeter firewall: deny-by-default, allow explicit outbound to redwood control plane (list endpoints as tags/env var), and allow node egress to package repositories (apt/yum/containers).
- Security groups should be as coarse as possible for infra (lb->nodes, nodes->internet for egress via NAT) but network ACLs used for emergency-wide block.
- Template example (text):
  - ALLOW tcp 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to nat-gateway
  - ALLOW tcp 853 from kube-system -> coredns cluster IPs (internal)
  - DENY all inbound except ssh from ops jump/managed bastions

Kubernetes network policies (bootstrap):
- Enforce default-deny at namespace level for new clusters. Provide module-managed YAML that can be applied during cluster bootstrap.
- Label convention: team=<team-name>, app=<app-name>. NetworkPolicy examples included as k8s manifest snippets.

Example NetworkPolicy (snippet):
```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
  namespace: platform
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress: []
```

Upgrade plan (high level):
1) Preflight: run terraform fmt, validate, terratest unit tests, and static checks (tfsec, checkov). Gather plan diff and annotate risk areas (routing changes, new NAT IPs, DNS changes).
2) Staging apply: apply to sandbox VPC (mirror customer's CIDR offsets) and run integration smoke tests.
3) Canary: for customer-managed infra, schedule a maintenance window; apply to a single AZ or subnet with low-traffic workloads first. For hosted VPCs, canary by customer account.
4) Full apply: run terraform apply with state locking. Monitor metrics for 30–60 minutes.
5) Post-check: DNS resolution for all private names, connectivity to control-plane endpoints, outbound path verification (curl to endpoints), and container image pulls.

Detailed engineering steps for a TF module bump that affects routing/NAT/DNS:
- Create release branch for tf-modules.
- Bump module version and add changelog entry explaining migration steps.
- Prepare migration plan file in repo with exact tf commands and variables to pass.
- Take tfstate snapshot and store with timestamped key (s3://redwood-state-backups/customer-xyz/...).
- Run `terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan` and upload plan artifact to PR.
- Schedule change window with customer.
- During apply: use `terraform apply "plan.tfplan"` with state lock. Watch route tables and whether any ephemeral rules were created.
- If ASG/node restarts required, cordon/drain nodes gracefully.

Rollback strategy:
- If connectivity/dns breaks: restore previous tfstate snapshot, `terraform apply` using pinned module ref (previous tag).
- For DNS zone mistakes: revert zone changes and re-associate previous zone; notify customer that DNS caches may require TTL expire.
- Record incident and preserve apply logs for postmortem.

Testing matrix and smoke checks (minimum automated list):
- DNS: dig @<resolver> internal-svc.<domain> -> expects A/AAAA/CNAME as defined.
- Egress: from a test pod, curl https://httpbin.org/ip and confirm SNAT ip in expected range.
- Firewall: attempt denied inbound port -> expect TCP RST/timeout.
- Network policies: create a pod with label legal and one without -> verify isolation per policy.
- Terratest cases: module variables boundary testing, import tests for existing zones (import aws_route53_zone into state and run apply idempotence).

Operational checks to run pre/post apply:
- Verify backend health and state locking service is healthy (DynamoDB/Consul).
- Confirm provider credentials (aws sts get-caller-identity) and permissions.
- Ensure route table associations as expected.

Monitoring and observability: what to watch after an apply:
- DNS resolution latency and NXDOMAIN spikes.
- Egress NAT IPs usage and errors (connection resets).
- Packet drop rates on critical load balancers or uplinks.
- K8s events for CNI/Coredns restarts and node kubelet issues.

Checklist before shipping this doc as a runbook:
- [ ] Add Terratest integration examples to module repo (owner: Liam).
- [ ] Document provider permission matrix (minimal perms) (owner: Noah).
- [ ] Author Confluence how-to with screenshots for AWS/GCP/Azure/on-prem (owner: Priya).
- [ ] Add automated Canary pipeline for tf-module releases.

Open questions / outstanding decisions:
- IPAM integration: should modules provision addresses from a centralized IPAM (netbox) or leave to customer? (impact: tracking NAT ranges and avoiding overlap).
- IPv6: roadmap TBD — want to add v6 variable options but need provider-specific testing.
- Shared VPC / multi-tenant: what constraints do enterprise customers require (single VPC with namespaces vs many VPCs)?
- On-prem appliance integration templates vary widely; we should collect 3 vendor patterns (F5, Checkpoint, Palo Alto) for example configs.

Notes to self / rough items:
- Keep example TF snippets minimal in this doc; link to module README for full usage.
- Add standard variable for `egress_audit_tag` so customers can tag flows for billing/observability.
- Double-check AWS private zone confirmation flow: association needs VPC ID; cross-account requires delegation.

Related artifacts: Confluence guide (linked), PRs in infra repo, JIRA ENGOPS-2387 (networking module refactor).

If you are editing this doc: leave TODOs inline, mark any blocker with [BLOCKER].

Contact & escalation:
- Slack: #infra-private-deployments, pager: on-call infra team.
- Primary owners: Priya Kapoor (runbook), Liam Chen (TF tests), Noah Patel (provider matrix).

End of draft.
